new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is initial in monosyllables and in vowel-final (open-ended) di- and trisyllabic words; in consonant-final (closed-ended) di- and trisyllabic words it falls on the second syllable; a syllable containing a diphthong attracts the stress wherever it is. Words longer than three syllables are said not to occur. Effectively a shape-conditioned rule (final-consonant and diphthong sensitivity) rather than a single fixed position; stress is not described as contrastive and no tone is mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Diphthong-bearing syllables take the stress regardless of position (examples /'poila/, /'gutei/ are both initial); no tetrasyllabic words found; no other exceptions given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolated citation forms; brief impressionistic statement (half a page) in a descriptive PhD thesis; no acoustic evidence, no discussion of phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Bhuyan 2013 describes Nefamese as the Assamese-based contact language of Arunachal Pradesh, data collected 2009-2012 from multilingual/bilingual informants (e.g. at Rajiv Gandhi University, Itanagar); same entity as Glottolog nefa1235. Saikia's Gauhati thesis calls it 'Arunachali-Asamiya' (Arunachali Assamese) = Nefamese, same variety.

sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonology, sec. 3.10 'Supra-segmental feature: Stress' (pp. 76-77): primary stress on the first syllable of monosyllables and of open-ended (vowel-final) di- and trisyllabic words; on the second syllable of closed-ended (consonant-final) di- and trisyllabic words; on the diphthong if the word contains one; no tetrasyllabic words found. No mention of tone or secondary stress.
